reviews.text: [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/31028489-Maddmike/]Maddmike Steam Curator[/url] There is a “what the hell am I playing” curve that frontloads any time spent with ‘Gods Against Machines’. For the first 30 minutes I thought I was experiencing some avant-garde clicker game and, honestly, that feeling only partially dissolved over the following eight hours. But I don’t intend ‘clicker’ as a pejorative. Gods Against Machines infuses that click-heavy progression fantasy with strategy and flow; with matches that emulate the back and forth tempo of real time strategy base-building without any of the micromanagement. The result is a roguelite God-game that plays something like an inverted RTS, where the fantasy isn’t building large armies and resource outposts but instead sending natural disasters to someone who is. It is satisfyingly destructive and deeper than its first few minutes implies, if a little finite by its genre standard. https://youtu.be/quhprCB0w9M The machines are taking over your world, and slowly spreading their corruption as they build more bases. Destroying enough of those bases leads to victory of that round and the ability to power up your spells so you can proceed to the next; and that spreading corruption acts as an implicit time limit to ensure you’re tactical about what you’re killing and when. The god you play is just one of four abstract concepts visualized by calamitous artwork in character select and nothing more. They each get a different element that strikes the earth with your clicks and a different set of actives and passives that change how they play. Shared among all gods is completely autonomous micromanagement. Your equivalent of a “base” is randomly spawning mana crystals that increase your resource generation, which give you greater power as the match goes on and something to defend from your opponents. If you’re playing the game right you’ll be spam clicking to bring destruction but quickly shifting your camera between their base and yours to ensure your mana reserves never get crippled. It’s almost like you’re pantomiming your way through an RTS, as if Gods Against Machines’ fantasy isn’t just one of playing god but also literally the fantasy of playing an RTS itself. You’ve got a real time strategy vocab list of stuff you wanna be thinking about like workers, economy, and tech trees but none of the execution demands those concepts are usually stapled to. It does make Gods Against Machines significantly easier than most of the games it looks like, but it’s not completely devoid of strategy. You still have all your build crafting and meta progression to think about; which requires picking and prioritizing spells complimentary to your regular ol’ clicks while also avoiding any resource bottlenecks from what those spells cost. Most of the mid-round strategy comes from smart target prioritization and attentiveness to your base, but there’s some subtle tricks the enemies employ that ask more than that. One of your earliest roadblocks won’t be standard damage prevention shields but click prevention zones that the enemy erects over key assets. An uncoordinated build will be forced to wait for their small recharge windows to strike but if you plan ahead you can either pick up some spells that pierce the zone, double down on automated minions that can swarm the zone, or even “Trojan Horse” some clicks through by leveraging traveling spells that can start their trajectory outside of the click-free-zone before bursting into it. That might be one of Gods Against Machines greatest assets: not just the destruction itself but the tension and release windows that give pace to that destruction. Any given round isn’t a steady increase of knocking down densely packed enemy buildings, but an alternation between nipping at their heels and devastating their strongholds. It’s a simple but enjoyable system, one that tempers your idler-like power increasing clicks with just enough roadblocks to overcome and make that progression feel meaningful. [h2] In Conclusion [/h2] It’s easy to accuse Gods Against Machines of being a little one note: there’s no alternate enemy factions nor varying bosses that end each major round, and spell selection is narrow enough that once you’ve identified a winning strategy for each god you can reliably recreate it on subsequent runs. For these reasons I don’t think the game has legs to be a “rogue” in the long term play fashion, it’s too easy to solve. It might be a little lightweight but the path to those solutions is satisfying and destructive. Its ‘contra-RTS’ gameplay style is a fun mix of god game and strategy. It’s gamified the feeling of kicking over someone else’s sandcastle: and though that feeling may be less rewarding and thoughtful than creating your own, it's hard to argue the visceral thrill of watching the grains of sand fly everywhere. Great game! It feels like a fun little half-auto-battler half-god-game where you try to destroy the ever expanding machine empire. You can build buildings that automatically generate units to attack them, cast spells to directly attack them, and so forth. Sometimes you fight a very silly Commander unit that does anime moves as the machines make their last stand. So the game has some jank, but overall I don't regret my purchase at all. And I recommend peeps try the demo first to see if it's something they'd like.

TLDR: If you told me there was an asymmetrical RTS rogue-like game, I would ask if you just picked random gamey-sounding words. But this game managed to pull it off amazingly. If you like RTS games (but maybe don't like the time commitment of a round like me) then you will probably like this game. It is almost like playing Age of Mythology but instead of micro-managing units, you have all of the god-powers and fight directly against the enemy. Rounds are super fast so it does not have the grind of a typical RTS game. Easy concept, but like a good rogue-like, gets challenging fast. Get this game if: -You like RTS games but sometimes get annoyed with micro-managing units. -You like the rogue-like style were every 'run' will play out differently based on chosen upgrades. - You liked turning on 'god-mode' in games and just smiting enemies with lightning bolts. Maybe avoid if: -You are hardcore into the micro-managing in an RTS. You don't directly build or control units here. -You don't like the randomness of rogue-like games. You get random upgrade choices after every round. Other Notes: What makes this game engaging is that it feels like the enemies adapt to your upgrades. I don't know how 'smart' the enemy is but I was rudely surprised when a strategy that I had been using was suddenly nullified by a new enemy building. My hatred for this new building made me irrationally target them as soon as possible. Now I am questioning if my divine rage would have been better focused somewhere else. It feels like powers can be used in creative ways. Powers also feel like they can be combined in clever ways to do devastating combos. Combined with different modifiers on each map a once powerful strategy may become useless and you will have to adapt. The game can be paused with the space bar. This is a simple but wonderful feature for people who may have interruptions around. The controls are pretty standard and were easy to pick up. I can see myself sinking a lot of time into this game, so glad I found it.

Recommended game, I've followed its development over time and I have to say it's one of the few really fun addictive games I've ever played, with a heavy dose of drugs from one game leading to another, so you have to be careful that one once you start... then it's hard to stop XD What is noteworthy are the passive and active skills that can be unlocked. I have rarely found such a level of depth and inventiveness in finding such enticing and well-made, as well as varied, upgrades. On the other hand, the game is very frenetic and it is difficult to follow the chaos that is generated during the fights, fortunately the games do not last long, but the idea of not having much control over the events and what happens is persistent. Another negative aspect is that the upgrades are many and with many points that can be distributed while on the other hand the upgrade points that are obtained are very few and for someone who likes to unlock as much as possible, it is something that leaves me quite disappointed, among one mission and another. In any case, I recommend it to you, both for the decidedly affordable price, and for the quality and attention that has gone into the development, and, and this is something worthy of praise, for the developer who is always present on the forum with whom it is possible to compare and improve the game together. I hope it is successful to see an even bigger next chapter :)

A neat little game that would be fun if it wasn't for the horrible balance. The only viable builds seem to be to just max your basic spell to ridiculousness. Every other spell is too slow and does tiny fractions of the potential of the default left-click. And don't even start with me about trying to get minions/summons viable. Even if you max them from the start they scale worse than the default enemies that are summoned by the dozens. Also the mechanic with the building that just doesn't let you cast is just awful. Hope you picked up a spell that just happens to not be affected by it, otherwise you can just stare at the building for a minute. The hints say to use minions but again they die instantly. And if two of them spawn covering each other one just becomes uncounterable so good luck with that map. The fun of roguelike games is to play with different builds and max out what seems to be good or fun. It's okay if some builds are better than others. It's not okay if 95% of the builds are just completely unviable.

The game's got a solid concept and it's fun to play, but it's not without its flaws. It's pretty easy—I managed to breeze through a max level run on my second try, even without many permanent upgrades that carry over. Those upgrades felt kind of worthless as a result. I would've 100% completed all achievements in about 6 hours, but I gave up on the last 2 after the game crashed on me three times mid-campaign, forcing me to start all over again. Even though I've got a decent rig, I still experienced major FPS drops when things got too hectic on screen, especially with end-game minion spamming builds. I had to dial down all settings just to keep the game running smoothly. More spells and upgrades, with better synergy between them, would definitely spice things up. Most upgrades just felt like boring number boosts that didn't really change up the gameplay or feel rewarding. But don't get me wrong—I still think the game's good and worth the money. I'm just pointing out these issues because I think the game's got so much potential, and I'd love to see it reach that. Edit 14/04/24 - 1.2 All issues i had the game were fixed and it's great, still feels a little easy even on the hardest setting but looking forward to whatever is added in the future :)

Do you like Mechs? Transformers? Macross? You like leading good Robots into Battle against evil? Then this Game is not for you. Sorry. This time you have to fight Machines. Welcome to GODS AGAINST MACHINES! A peacefull Planet is going to be invaded by an evil Robot Army. Their buildings are creating a corruption that is spreading all over the Planet, taking over. Now it is up to the Planets Goddess Gaia ... and you. Get ready to beat the hell out of the Invaders. GODS AGAINST MACHINES is something really unique. A Realtime Strategy Roguelike Shoot´em Up Game. Yes, i know how strange this sounds but it works. In the beginning you can choose one of 4 Gods, each with special abilities. And this Choice will decide how you play. Will you fight with destruction spells or will you call Minions or something else? Find your own style. Gaia shows her presence in form of Mana Crystalls growing all over the Map. This Crystalls will give you the Power to cast your spell. So, defend them as good as you can. And of course you have to destroy every Machine Presence. Destroy Terraformer to lower or stop the corruption, defend your Units against their Troops, get high Rewards for your progress and sometimes when the Machines are near defeat a Boss is spawning. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3171832476 That is all in Realtime and it surprisely works wonderfull. Oldschool Player may remember the Games POPULOUS or MEGA LO MANIA. There you are also a god and your decisions influence your Area. You have no directly controll over your Units like in RTS like COMMAND & CONQUER. Summoned, they do what they are designed for. You can for example defend them, like the big Crab you summon to only destroy Buildings. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3171832717 To be honest, in the first Hour i was wildly clicking on the Buildings and enemy Units, but the more i played, the more i recognized how good Strategy is in the right way. The better you complete a Map with for example the lowest Corruption, the better the Rewards. You can raise your Spells and also Gaias abilities. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3171832935 The Graphics are very well done and the Performance is great. No matter how many Units i´ve got on my Screen, no juddering. The Sounds are great and that goes also for the fantastic Soundtrack. GODS AGAINST MACHINES is a nice Suprise in the Ocean of Games. Realtime Strategy with fast Rounds without big Micromanagement. Good old little POPULOUS and MEGA LO MANIA Vibes. Easy to learn, later harder to master. Just start and enjoy. Thanks to the DEVS for this nice Game. As a Fan of Mechs i´m hoping for a DLC for changing Roles: MACHINES AGAINST GODS. What do you think, dear Reader? This game is his 9,75 Euros absolutly worth. What are you waiting for? Thank you for reading.

Game is quite a bit easy, after you play with all them gods and get to level 99 in void, there isn't anything else to do. After playing [b]the demo[/b], I went into [i]Gods against Machines[/i] with [b]tempered expectations[/b]. Between obvious AI art, stock GUI scheme (the same one [i]Fractured Online[/i] uses), very indistinct art direction, seemingly unsophisticated gameplay, and [i]"right click for unit info"[/i] straigh tup not working, I fully expected a gaming equivalent of a supermarket hot dog. It might not be great, but sometimes a cheap hot dog is what you need to scratch a particular itch. Unfortunately, it seems it's one of these games where the demo cuts off right before the game gets bad. [h1]Fake difficulty by going uninteractive[/h1] [i]GvM[/i] is basically a game about using god-game rules to fight an enemy that uses standard RTS rules, where you need to make it lose enough resources before it generates enough [strike]Victory Points[/strike] Corruption to win. As in, you don't control any units, and your entire input is constantly blasting with your basic attack spell, and rarely blasting a Bigger Badder Attack or summoning a Bigger Badder Unit. You have spells that create temporary artillery pieces and unit spawners - but you can and should set them to autocast, since manual casting can't make any difference with them other than missing the perfect cooldown. The issue is that when you go past the levels included in the demo, the game starts overusing anti-magic fields - areas where you can't cast spells - and the game [b]grinds to a halt and becomes barely interactable[/b]. You see the distinctive anti-magic building getting constructed and you can't destroy it before it's completed, because buidlings under construction get 90% damage reduction. You then can't do anything to attack the enemy factories and Corruption-generators inside the field (wide-area spells don't have enough reach to hit it, and "elite" summons have neither strength nor determination to attack the center), so you go to destroy the few buildings outside and - OH LOOK, another anti-magic building is getting constructed! Obviously, this means you should go on the defensive and provide covering fire to your own units so they can attack - OH LOOK, enemy assault is protected by units that [i]also[/i] have a anti-magic field! I've seen about 30 different spells so far, and only one (1) of them counters the anti-magic field, and I've seen if offered exactly once. And there weren't any anti-magic-penetrating spell upgrades either. So - unless you had the extreme luck to even see the spell and the precognition to pick it - you basically have to sit down and wait until your units get lucky, or the enemy constructs enough stray buildings outside the anti-magic field for you to chip away the enemy's resources. I'd be fine with the game remaining an unchallenging cakewalk, and I'd be fine with the game getting challenging by adding depth, but I'm not fine with the game getting "difficult" by locking the player out. Especially since the rest of the game seems low-effort, too. ...and I haven't even mentioned the anti-magic fields are represented by yellow-orange dotted line on the ground that is very hard to make out.

I don't really know how to feel about this game. The wind god seems by far the best and this was my first run which probably ruined it for all the other gods. The wind god has a huge advantage over all the other ones - being able to easily strike enemy air units. This is more important in the early game and playing all the other gods simply isn't as fun because it's way harder to play them. Don't feel like there's much replayability, I have no reason to play 100 levels again with constant clicking and basically no breaks. This game is not that hard IF you don't break for a single second in a level. If you want to sit back and relax in a map, this game is not for you. It's really hectic and requires constant action.

First thing first, this game is NOT an RTS game at all, so if you just want to play an RTS, you may just turn away now. The game is, for lack of a better description, a City Destroyer Survivors semi-action roguelite. Yep IMHO the core gameplay mechanics is more like Vampire Survivors than a strategy game. It's more or less about getting to an overpowered build and wreak havoc with spectacular spell effects on enemy hordes that keeps getting stronger wave after wave. Except the waves here are split into regions. The most important thing in this game is to choose the right spells combinations with the right spell upgrades, and the right blessings, to synergize into some super powerful build that can crush the enemy bases/cities. And the fun of the game is more about trying out all kinds of different builds, as there are 60+ spells and 60+ blessings, while you can only have 5 to 7 spells and 10 or so blessings in one run, that's actually a lot of replayability (not to the level of Vampire Survivors or Slay the Spire, but still I'd imagine easily 100+ hours). The game itself is not that challenging (so are VS and StS when you know what builds you are aiming for), but there are quite some varieties in different play styles and, on higher difficulty levels, you do need to plan for some good spells+upgrades+blessings combo with good synergy to really become the overpowered god that can pulverize the machine invasion. Also a lot of the fun is in exploring and challenging oneself with different builds, maxed Meteor Storm/Thunder Storm with Wormhole+Call Servant makes the run too easy? Then try not to pick those spells, maybe try Immortal Phoenix and Lava Nest, that will drastically change the way of how the game would play out. Your play style could end up as crazy clicking to destroy everything with your basic spell (with some disruptive spells to remove shields and anti-magic zones), or summoning super powerful monsters that stomp enemy units and level buildings, or just a couple well placed fire and forget WMD spells that you can then sit back and watch a large enemy area getting cleaned up, or gather a swarm of smaller beasts to overwhelm the enemy, etc. etc. The plot is next to non-existent, AFAIK it's about humans building interstellar army trying to colonize a fantasy themed planet, and you are a god protecting the fantasy planet and trying to defeat the human terraformer army. And that's it. So don't look for much (or any) story in this game. One thing is that the time it takes to complete one run is quite long compared to VS and StS, as it takes about 3 hours or so to clear the 99 regions in a run (that is, if you know what you are doing and aiming for a good build, else it may take much longer), so it takes more time to try out a different build, which may be annoying to some (it takes only 30 min to try out a new build in a VS run for comparison, however here you can finish a bunch regions, exit, and then continue later). So the overall pace is slower and more casual, which may or may not be a bad thing depending on the player. Also it helps to read through the description of spells in the Gods section of the main menu (which is more or less the manual/encyclopedia for the game), so that you can plan your build better. When I first played the air god, I got wormhole upgrade for the basic spell, so I presumed that all basic spells would have the wormhole upgrade, only then to find out that the fire god basic spell cannot have wormhole and I passed on wormhole upgrade for other spells, which makes the run quite painful as I have little counter-measure against anti-magic zones. There are rare cases when you have extremely bad luck in a run, where you just don't get some of the spells or upgrades you need for the planned build (for example no wormhole upgrades nor disruptive spells against anti-magic zones), that the run may become unenjoyable, but then that's true for most roguelike games when you just have some bad luck trying to get the skills/upgrades/weapons that you need the most. I think one questionable design of the game is to click and hold for 3 seconds to get the basic spell auto-fire, IMHO 3 seconds is too long, and many times 3 seconds of continuous firing already get the target destroyed, I'd hope there could be some other way to activate the basic spell auto-fire. Oh well I don't use the basic spells too much anyway, as I prefer builds where I don't need to click too much :p All in all if you take this game as a semi-action roguelite, that plays somewhat like a slower-paced Vampire Survivors in a skin that looks like an RTS, it's quite fun and can have a lot of replayability. But if you expect some real strategy game, or something really fast paced, then this game is not for you.

Gods Against Machines is another gem for me this year. Playing through each of the four factions, I racked up 15 hours of playtime, so you'll get roughly four hours fir each faction (on Normal). There seems to be a lot of confusion as to what this game is in the reviews, which makes sense, but I'd say it's Command & Conquer, but you can auto-build your troop-producing buildings with a right-click, and each will auto-build their respective unit for a length of time; beyond that, you have an arsenal of abilities--a primary elemental attach and 2+ powerful spells--selected a-la "pick one out of three" rewards. Once you get into the flow of the game, it become very fun and addicting. Combining WASD camera controls and certain powers as you click can feel devastatingly effective as you level entire armies in a single stroke. Once you learn the debuffs of the enemy, you learn effective methods to counter them, and due to the random nature of the game, generally find a good path forward that may be a unique experience from your regular playstyle. You must clear 40 levels, and there are various gameplay mechanics that force you to balance stopping at every level to collect rewards or to skip ahead to harder enemies to prevent the spread of Corruption, the game's timer mechanic. Corruption is done effectively; basically, you gain Corruption in each map as you play (unless you cleanse it) and that accumulates into the World Corruption pool. If that hits 100%, it's game over. Play well on each map and you can collect a lot of rewards, of which only the Gaia powerups carry over. This is my main pain point with the title as, once I came back to an element I had already completed, I found the elemental abilities had reset completely. I'm now at ~16 hours and feel that was well-spent but, attempting to convince myself the meager Gaia points alone will be worth my playtime, I decided to write this review instead. I understand the need of this mechanic as the game currently sits, but I was hoping you would cease to receive rewards in Normal once you beat it on a certain element, and would need to progress to the next tier of difficulty to continue receiving permanent rewards. The Gaia abilities are fine, but they're more like buffs (they lack acute interest), and it will take me roughly 4-8 hours of playtime to get my spider buildings to produce 1 spider every 24 seconds to 1 spider every 14 seconds (and that effect alone to carry over), and I just can't rationalize that compared to the other abilities carrying over, as well. Still, incredibly worth it! The game is a value even at full price, does so much right, and I recommend it to anyone interested (there's a free demo if you're somehow on the fence). And there is a Continue mode after you complete a run, so if you enjoy the build you have, you can keep on playing (this is likely what I'll eventually do). But to get here you must clear 40 levels prior and build your deck from there. I kind of wish there were a fully separate game mode (I'd even pay for DLC to further support the team) that allowed us to select ANY Rewards we've unlocked in the main game, at the highest level for each spell and buff, and use that in another run. It'd be neat if it allowed us to mix and match in this mode, selecting whatever powers and bonuses we want. The RNG of the main game if fun, but every good god game deserves to have the ability to build your own arsenal.

Very neat idea, I like the concept, but I'm not a fan of the slog. Some spells are WAYYYYYYYYYY better than others, like you pick the wrong one and you had might as well just restart because it isn't fun in an "experimental" way, it's just completely under-powered. It's also very repetitive right now, spamming the same spell and sometimes one of the other 2 or 3 spells you get over dozens of stages. You don't build units, sometimes you can create spawners that will make units but it's mainly just your spells. With balancing updates, more interactivity, and maybe an adjustment to how many spells you get, then it will be a bit more playable.
https://youtu.be/PVEv7rJE1vs Even with a compelling setup the gameplay lacks hooks and levers for the play to pull on creating an experience that is easily reduced to holding down a button.

I like the game and the ideas it presents. there is a good amount of depth and replayability. where I can't recommend it is in the controls. there is an autocast but its annoying, slow, cumbersome, does more harm than good and only applies to your very first main ability. more often than not I would find that the autocast I thought was locked onto a building I wanted dead was instead just pounding the ground wasting my mana. this led to me turning the feature off entirely even though its basically required for your sanity and fingers. immediately I can think of several ways this could be done better. double click toggles autocast. pressing a specific key with the selected skill and cursor location locks the attack into that location until you press the key again. really anything besides hold down the mouse for 3 entire seconds and hope you got the target right. the first like 13 victories I just kept saying wtf over and over as I slowly learned what the game was about. the map is sprawling and the minimap lends you no hints about special bushes to destory or whatever is going on. only icons for you, the enemy and the special spirit building thing that spawns. the sprawling map would like to have you look around it for that nonsense when theres really nothing going on except maybe in later stages and with more upgrades, so doing this early on is almost entirely a waste of time, all time should be spent just clicking their corruption producing buildings over and over and over. the nature of the game is fairly automated but it demands so much clicking from the player, eventually I got a powerful build and was skipping whole stage ranges at a time, bit off more than I could chew eventually when I got to the buildings where you cant cast in their aoe. I want to play again but then I remember how much clicking I was doing. you can actually overcome the cooldown or supposed max speed of the autocast simply by clicking, this immediately renders the autocast null and void and basically forces you to click as fast as possible if you want the best result in this game. if you do wish to pursue this game I honestly recommend setting up some kind of auto clicker. it's a shame because nearly everything else I think is interesting about the game and wouldn't mind progressing with it and unlocking stuff but playing\controlling it is simply mind numbing endurance

Great idea, hampered by flat execution. What could be great strategy game, with long term planning and building, is reduced to essentially clicker or mobile game, that could be playing itself. Spell selection is underwhelming and has too many similarities between elements. Progression system is grind for +1% more of XYZ. RNG is make or break at beginning and pointless later on, since grinded resources can offset it. Meanwhile missions are all the same scheme, repeated over and over. Same units, same bosses, same buildings just with more HP. Game shows all it has at the start and has little later on to make it worthwhile.
Didn't know what to expect from this game. Though was pleasently surprised. I find it to be a relaxing game with plenty of content. A little bit repetative. Though satisfying.

Overall, I like this game. It does have some issues as others mention in their reviews but IMO it pulls through despite them. Though I was on the fence until I tried my 3rd god and went in a completely different direction than the first two and had fun with it. Try the demo if you're still unsure.

Fun enough for the price, but honestly rather poorly balanced. There are absolutely several spells that are complete lemons and worthless no matter how you upgrade them, and some spells that will singlehandedly carry you through the entire campaign. The result is a very swingy experience, where you either sweep the entire game trivially or fail miserably in the first 20 regions.

At first it's a bit overwhellming with all different abilities, things like corruption reduction, and all the different enemy buildings. But when you get the hang of it and expanded your arsenal, even Brutal difficulty is a walk in the park. Hint: Read the hints during loadingscreens, they are usefull!!

It is as janky as the negative reviews suggest, but I'm not letting that get in my way of having a good time. I can't put it down - although it obviously not a 'play forever' type game. Going to have fun beating it with every elemental god, then be on may way
